text: Hello, everyone. My name's Elizabeth Oliphant. I'm gonna start sharing my screen and this presentation. So, yeah. Okay. Can all of you see my screen? Yeah. I'll get started then. And this was an analysis of the total utility costs for electrifying single family residences in Palo Alto. Yeah. So a little bit of the motivation behind this project. The main goal for electrifying single family homes is to reduce the greenhouse gas emissions and thus help Palo Alto stick to the SCAP goals that have been laid out. And the scope of this project was single family residence in Palo Alto, of which there are about 15,000. And tonight I'm gonna be presenting on the utility costs, which include upgrading the electrical system and disconnecting gas lines in the city of Palo Alto. So first off, what is electrification? It's replacing all of those residential gas appliances with all electric appliances. So this means that your water heater will become a heat pump water heater instead of a traditional gas water heater. The stoves will become induction cooktops and gas dryers will be replaced with electric dryers, as well as gas heating systems will be replaced with air source heat pumps. So first I'm gonna talk about the electrical upgrades associated with this change. So electrifying all of those gas appliances will increase the peak electricity demand by almost three times. And as you can see in this graph on the left, it will be a winter peaking load, mainly due to heating and those air source heat pumps. The blue line is a mixed fuel house and the orange line is an all electric. So it's almost three times a higher peak demand and it also is gonna be a higher annual energy use. So this will affect different customer bills. So a little bit of an overview about the electrical system in the city of Palo Alto. So the city of Palo Alto utilities is largely not in charge of generating their own electricity. This is handled by outside companies and along with the long range transmission, the city of Palo Alto buys its electricity at different substations around the city. And then using primary feeders that are higher voltage transmits this electricity throughout the city has different transformers that step down the electricity and then transmit it to houses. So with a higher peak demand, many of those transformers will need to be upgraded. So to determine how many transformers will need to be upgraded, I looked at the appliance load increases and a potential for EV load as well. So for EV load, there were two scenarios that I considered. One was an optimistic flexible load. And in this scenario, the peak demand did not increase with additional electric vehicles. So instead of a higher load, it was just the load that you saw in the slides before, which was about three times the current load. For the more conservative EV scenario, I added 9.74 kilowatts per transformer. And this number comes from an estimate of how much the average Palo Alto residents drive, that we are assuming high EV penetration. So about two EVs per house and about eight houses per transformer. So in both scenarios, I found that over 95% of the around 800 transformers that are serving single family residences will be overcapacity. And these overcapacity transformers can be replaced in two different ways. They can either be replaced with a like for like upgrade. So one pad mounted transformer becomes two pad mounted transformers or maybe three. Or it can be an optimized upgrade, which means that a pole mounted transformer can become a pad mounted transformer and thus be able to withstand a higher capacity. So to determine the number of transformers needed, I looked at that increased load and then scaled it based on that. Costs for the transformer upgrades. If we go with the like for like upgrade strategy, we're looking at a minimum cost in the optimistic flexible load scenario of around $12.5 million and a maximum cost in the conservative scenario of around $32.9 million. If we do optimize upgrades, we're looking at a minimum cost of around $8.3 million for the optimistic flexible load scenario and the maximum cost for the conservative scenario of around $25.4 million. And once again, this optimized scenario is upgrading a pole mounted with perhaps a pad mounted or a different type of transformer. There are also gonna be other electrical upgrades that will need to happen with this increased load. So around 20% of the secondary transmission lines are expected to be overcapacity and these costs anywhere between 30 and $50,000 per secondary transmission line to replace. Additionally, around 25% of the feeder lines are expected to be overcapacity and these are much more expensive to replace at a cost of one to $2 million. So for these other upgrades, we're looking at anywhere from $21.4 million to $41.7 million. There also are going to be costs associated with the gas disconnection. So for the gas disconnection, we are looking at disconnecting all 15,000 single family residents, but this does not mean the entire gas system will be removed. Instead, a skeleton gas system will remain throughout the city and connect those commercial customers with the gas system and multifamily customers as well. So in terms of what types of disconnections we're looking at there's three main types. You have main lines, which in the picture on the right, you can see it's that larger yellow line labeled one. So that's a main line and these connect multiple houses to the gas system. Then there are service lines, which connect to individual houses and that's labeled two on the graph on the right. And then each house also has a meter and riser. So all of the estimates you're about to see come from a estimate of $640 per hour, which covers a four person crew and all the overhead expenses associated with this crew. Something I want to stress is that the costs per hour will be different if outside contractors are used instead of CPAU staff. So a bit more on the gas disconnection. In the picture on the right, you can see more of these main lines, which as I said before, are larger pipes that serve several customers. And these mains are usually sealed at the valves, which are these circles that you can see at the different corners. So sealing a main at a valve disconnects all the service lines that are connected to the main. But something that's critical to note is that all customers have to agree to disconnection to be able to seal that main. So if one customer does not want to disconnect, it can either delay the project or make it so the main cannot be sealed. And service lines connect to individual houses. And I considered two different scenarios for service lines, depending on if customers agree to disconnection all at the same time or if they do not. And then in all cases, every single family residence meter and riser will need to be disconnected by a professional meter technician. So for the costs, in both of the scenarios that I considered, 1,640 mains are gonna be sealed and all 15,008 meters and risers will need to be sealed. For the optimistic scenario, I determined that only houses on the skeleton gas system will need their service line disconnected individually. So this means that around 2,500 service lines will need to be sealed individually. Because as I said before, once you seal a main at a valve, it automatically disconnects the service lines on that main. In the more conservative scenario, I said that all houses will need their service lines disconnected individually. So all 15,000, so much larger number. In terms of total costs, for the optimistic case, we're looking at a minimum of 11,000 or 11,400,000 and a maximum of $16.7 million. For the conservative case, we're looking at anywhere from 31.2 million to 53.7 million. So there is a large range in these costs, but it likely is going to fall somewhere in the middle because some customers will agree to disconnection and others will not. There also are large cost savings associated with sealing up the mains. So CPAU runs a gas main replacement program which aims to replace two to four miles of PVC piping every single year. So by preemptively sealing up these PVC pipes, we can avoid the costs associated with replacing them, which aren't small. For the 23 miles of gas PVC mains and service lines, we can estimate there'll be a saving of anywhere from 26 to 34 million, which if you remember from the costs on the slide before, that is around the costs for the optimistic scenario of sealing up all these pipes. So the grand total that we have to electrify single-family residence, it's going to cost the utility anywhere from $41.1 million to $128.3 million.
